Rangpur Police, bKash hold workshop to prevent online gambling, fraud, and criminal activities
item.description:
As part of ongoing efforts to make Mobile Financial Services (MFS) more secure while preventing their misuse in online gambling, fraud, and other criminal activities, a workshop titled “Investigation and Prevention of Misuse of Mobile Financial Services” was held in Rangpur.
A total of 45 investigating officers of the district police attended this daylong workshop, organized by Rangpur district police and bKash, at the police lines hall room.
The workshop sheds light on how law enforcement can leverage transactional data to identify criminal gangs and bring them to justice.
To date, 4,500 officials from various law enforcement bodies have benefited from these sessions held across the country.
Mohammad Mozammel Haque, Superintendent of Police, Rangpur, attended the workshop as chief guest.
On behalf of bKash, EVP and head of external affairs Major AKM Monirul Karim (retd) was present at the workshop.
The workshops featured detailed discussions on leveraging technology to track customers’ lost funds, preventing offences such as online gambling, fraud, and kidnapping through digital transaction monitoring, and establishing swift communication channels between investigating officers and bKash officials.
In particular, the session highlighted how MFS transaction data can be utilized to trace financial trails and apprehend individuals or syndicates involved in online gambling and other cybercrimes.
Additionally, the session emphasized immediate protocols to follow when a criminal incident occurs.
Notably, every transaction can be monitored and tracked as each digital transaction leaves a footprint.
This allows investigative bodies, including the Police, DB, CID, and PBI, to carry out the investigation process more accurately. In this regard, bKash has been continuously organizing workshops titled “Investigation and Prevention of Mobile Financial Services Misuse” with different stakeholders since 2017.

item.title: Toffee extends World Cup success into new EPL season
item.description:
Toffee will be carrying forward its record-breaking Fifa World Cup 2026 streaming success by live streaming the 2026-27 English Premier League Season (EPL).
All league matches can be streamed live by Toffee subscribers in Full HD.
Football fans have been eagerly waiting to watch their favorite players back on the pitch following the world cup season.
The wait comes to an end with the beginning of the 35th season of English Premier League where fans will find their favorite players back in action.
Building on this momentum, Toffee is now bringing the full 2026-27 English Premier League (EPL) season to viewers, with matches taking place across 38 weeks.
Toffee subscribers can now buy the EPL Pass for Tk649 to get full tournament access, which will last for ten months and is valid for all 380 matches.
Toffee subscribers buying this pack will be able to live stream the entire season on three devices in full HD.
On the other hand, Toffee is also offering the short EPL Pass for Tk99 for 30 days, through which Toffee subscribers will also be able to live stream the matches in full HD and this pack will also be supported in three devices.
Toffee subscribers will also be able to watch other football tournaments such as UEFA Champions Legue, Bundesliga and The FA Cup through the platform’s international TV channels and all these matches can be viewed live.
The viewers will need to keep an eye on the Toffee app to be notified about all the upcoming contents.
Commenting on the initiative, Modasser Ahmed, head of Toffee, Banglalink, said: “The Fifa World Cup 2026 was a defining moment for Toffee, with millions of football fans choosing our platform to experience the biggest tournament in the world. We are excited to build on this momentum as we bring another season of the Premier League to Toffee viewers across Bangladesh. With a strong focus on delivering a seamless and engaging viewing experience, we look forward to making this EPL season another memorable one for Toffee users.”
Subscribers can sign up through the Toffee app or website to avail themselves of their preferred EPL pass.
They can also enjoy a wide range of entertainment content, including movies, dramas, live sports and other digital content on Toffee.

item.title: Bangladeshi among 22 missing after cargo ship sinks off India
item.description:
An Indian coastguard and navy search-and-rescue operation was underway on Sunday for 22 people, including a Bangladeshi national, who went missing after a Panama-flagged bulk carrier sank off India’s eastern coast, Reuters reported.

Two Chinese crew members were rescued after the Ocean Winner, carrying 24 crew, sank on Friday. The vessel developed a list and went down within eight minutes, forcing the crew to abandon ship, Shyam Jagannathan, director general of India’s Maritime Administration, told Reuters.

The missing crew include 18 Chinese nationals, three Myanmar nationals and one Bangladeshi, according to the Indian Coast Guard.

The ship was carrying iron ore to China after departing from Paradip port. It sank about 240 nautical miles from the port. The cause of the sinking was not immediately known.

Indian naval and coastguard vessels are continuing the search for the missing crew members.

Andaleeve vows to support media, not control it
item.description:
Newly appointed Information and Broadcasting Minister Andaleeve Rahman on Sunday pledged to take the media forward through cooperation rather than control, stressing the importance of ensuring credible communication of government activities to the people.
He made the remarks at a view-exchange meeting with officials of the ministry and its subordinate departments and agencies at the Secretariat on his first working day after assuming office.
“The responsibility of credibly communicating all government activities to the people is a very big one for us. At the same time, we have to keep in mind our relationship with the people and the issue of national unity,” the minister said.
He said the ministry also has a responsibility to preserve the country’s cultural and religious values, the spirit of the Liberation War and other sources of national pride.
Describing the current period as one of the most difficult times in Bangladesh’s history, Andaleeve said the government is making every possible effort under the leadership of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.
“Everyone can make mistakes. But from the standpoint of ethics, we are in a very strong position,” he said, adding that the government’s instruction under the prime minister’s leadership is to serve the country and advance the interests of the people.
Describing the media as one of the most important pillars of democracy, the minister said the media helped people learn about government failures, irregularities and repression despite various forms of control and restrictions over the past 17 years.
“There is no way to underestimate the role of the media during the July movement. Their role was important in every respect,” he said, stressing that the ministry’s role should be regulatory rather than controlling.
“We have to keep in mind that we are responsible for regulating this ministry, but in no way should we go into control,” Andaleeve said.
He also said ethical decline and structural problems have developed in various state institutions over the past 17 years.
The minister said repairing the damage caused to the judiciary, politics, statutory bodies, Parliament and other institutions will take time, but everyone must remain aware of the paths that should not be taken. “We have to concentrate on repairing the damage and developing a new system,” he said.

item.title: Health minister reimburses patient after finding saline withheld despite stock
item.description:
Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain on Saturday reimbursed a patient from his pocket after finding that the patient was asked to buy saline from outside despite the item being available in the stock of Naogaon General Hospital.
He made a surprise visit to the hospital around 10:30am and inspected different wards, the operating theatre, pharmacy and kitchen. He also spoke to patients during his hour-long inspection.
During the visit, the minister expressed dissatisfaction after learning that a nurse asked a patient to purchase saline from outside despite its availability in the hospital stock. He reimbursed the patient for the cost of the saline from his pocket and instructed the hospital authorities to investigate the matter.
After completing the inspection, the minister went to the office of the hospital superintendent and called doctors who were absent from duty on their mobile phones, seeking explanation for their absence.
Talking to journalists later, Sakhawat said he found irregularities during the inspection, including the failure to provide patients with saline available in the hospital stock. He said a doctor was also found absent from duty and the hospital authorities were warned over the irregularities.
“The government has taken various initiatives to ensure healthcare services for people at the grassroots level,” the minister said.
He said the government is also planning to install 50 dialysis beds at every medical college hospital and 10 beds at each district-level general hospital so that patients do not have to travel to Dhaka for tertiary-level dialysis treatment.
“At the district level, there will be 60 dialysis machines. We hope if each of the 60 machines can provide three rounds of dialysis a day, they will be able to serve 180 patients daily,” the minister said.
He added that facilities, including the number of beds, will soon be expanded at upazila health complexes across the country.

item.title: LNG supply to national grid rises, easing gas shortage
item.description:
The supply of liquefied natural gas (LNG) from two floating terminals in Maheshkhali of Cox’s Bazar has increased, providing some relief amid the country’s ongoing gas shortage.
At noon Saturday, the two terminals were supplying a combined 740 million cubic feet (mmcfd) of gas to the national grid. Officials said the supply would be increased gradually.
Engineer Muhammad Nasir Uddin, deputy general manager at the Chittagong office of Rupantarita Prakritik Gas Company Ltd (RPGCL), said that LNG supply from the two floating terminals in Maheshkhali had resumed and was being increased in phases.
He said an LNG carrier carrying a shipment from the United States began unloading at the Floating Storage and Regasification Unit (FSRU) operated by Excelerate Energy around 9:30pm on Saturday.
The terminal had remained out of operation for three days before resuming limited gas supply from its existing stock around 2pm on Saturday. Initially, it supplied 100 mmcfd to the national grid. By noon yesterday, the supply had increased to 240 mmcfd.
At the same time, Summit LNG Terminal was supplying 500 mmcfd, bringing the combined supply from the two terminals to 740 mmcfd.
Excelerate Energy’s terminal was shut down following a fire incident on July 21. Although the terminal was fully prepared to resume LNG supply on August 15, the arrival of a new LNG cargo was delayed. As a result, the terminal initially resumed limited supply using its existing stock.
Following Excelerate Energy’s shutdown, Summit LNG Terminal had been supplying gas above its normal capacity to help meet national demand. However, Summit was also forced to suspend supply temporarily after running out of LNG.

item.title: Sunil Shuvo Roy appointed co-chairman, spokesperson of JaPa faction
item.description:
Sunil Shuvo Roy has been appointed co-chairman of the Jatiya Party (JaPa) faction led by Barrister Anisul Islam Mahmud.
He has also been given the responsibility of serving as the party’s spokesperson.
According to a press release issued by the party, the decision was taken at an emergency meeting held at the JaPa chairman’s office in Gulshan, Dhaka, on Sunday. Party Chairman Anisul Islam Mahmud and Secretary General ABM Ruhul Amin Howlader assigned Roy the new responsibilities.
Roy previously served as press secretary to JaPa founder and former chairman Hussain Muhammad Ershad. He also served as a member of the party’s presidium.
Following Ershad’s death, Roy remained with the faction led by Raushan Ershad. On Sunday, he rejoined the faction led by Anisul Islam Mahmud.
The meeting also discussed the ongoing gas and power crisis in the country.
JaPa Secretary General ABM Ruhul Amin Howlader said the gas crisis was disrupting production at various industrial units, forcing some factories to shut down and leaving workers unemployed.
“The gas and power crisis is not only hurting the industrial sector, but also affecting employment, production, trade and the livelihoods of ordinary people,” he said.
“Many industrial units are unable to maintain normal production due to the gas shortage. Production has declined in some factories, while others are being forced to shut down. When factories close, workers suffer the most as they lose their jobs, affecting their families as well.”
Calling for urgent action, Howlader said the crisis should not be underestimated.
“Factory closures do not mean losses for individual businesses alone. The livelihoods of thousands of workers, the future of their families and the country’s economy are all at stake. The government must give the issue immediate attention and take effective measures to resolve the gas and power crisis,” he said.
Senior JaPa Co-Chairman Kazi Firoz Rashid, Executive Chairman Mujibul Haque Chunnu, Presidium Members Jasim Uddin Bhuiyan and Sardar Md Shahjahan, along with other central leaders, also spoke at the meeting.

item.title: Off-season watermelon cultivation brings success to Dumuria farmer
item.description:
Off-season watermelon cultivation has brought significant success to a farmer in Dumuria upazila of Khulna, encouraging other local farmers to take up the high-value crop.
Mrityunjay Mondal, a farmer from Chhotoband village in Sahas union, has cultivated watermelon on 40 decimals of land using the trellis method. His field is now filled with mature watermelons hanging from the trellises.
“I was initially worried about growing watermelon in the off-season. But with proper advice from the agriculture office and regular care, I have achieved a good yield,” Mrityunjay said.
He said off-season watermelons have strong demand in the market and fetch a good price.
According to the farmer, he cultivated the Astha variety at a total cost of Tk20,000. He expects to initially sell around 42 maunds of watermelon at Tk50 per kilogram, generating about Tk84,000. He expects to earn another Tk25,000 from the remaining produce.
This would bring his estimated total sales to Tk109,000 and a potential net profit of around Tk89,000.
“My success has encouraged other farmers in the area to become interested in off-season watermelon cultivation using the trellis method,” he said.
Dumuria Upazila Agriculture Officer Agriculturist Md Nazmul Huda said the Department of Agricultural Extension had provided farmers with improved seeds, regular field visits and technical support for modern trellis-based cultivation.
“Despite salinity and adverse weather conditions, farmers like Mrityunjay have achieved good production through hard work and proper cultivation techniques,” he said.
Md Nazrul Islam, deputy director of the Department of Agricultural Extension in Khulna, said off-season watermelon cultivation was opening up new economic opportunities for farmers in the coastal region.
“Compared to conventional crops such as rice, off-season watermelon can provide significantly higher returns. We are encouraging farmers across the district to adopt modern technologies and cultivate high-value crops,” he said.
The successful harvest in Dumuria has created fresh prospects for off-season watermelon cultivation in the area, with more farmers expected to become interested in the practice.

item.title: Kurigram farmers break into dealer’s warehouse, take away 197 sacks of fertilizer
item.description:
Farmers broke into a fertiliser dealer’s warehouse and took away 197 sacks of urea and MOP fertiliser in Kurigram’s Bhurungamari upazila on Sunday, alleging an artificial shortage and overcharging.
The incident occurred around noon at Dhaldanga Bazar in Shilkhuri Union.
Police and local BNP leaders were present at the scene when the farmers broke through the warehouse’s tin fencing and took the fertiliser.
Additional police later arrived and brought the situation under control. By the afternoon, 58 of the 197 sacks had been returned, while most of the fertiliser remained unaccounted for.
According to locals, preparations were underway to distribute fertiliser at M/s Shah Amanat Enterprise, a BCIC-authorised dealer in the union. Four police personnel and local BNP leaders were present during the distribution.
Several farmers alleged that they had been visiting the dealer for days but were unable to obtain fertiliser. They claimed the dealer was selling part of the union’s allocated supply to retail traders, leaving farmers unable to buy enough fertiliser.
They also alleged that a sack priced at Tk1,300 was being sold by traders for Tk1,800–1,900, causing losses to farmers and threatening their crops.
Taifur Rahman Mukul, proprietor of M/s Shah Amanat Enterprise, said preparations were underway to distribute fertiliser when several people surrounded him and broke through the warehouse fencing.
“Farmers took away 197 sacks of urea and MOP fertiliser. The situation became so tense that police and the administration struggled to control it,” he said, adding that he would file a case over the incident.
Upazila Agriculture Officer Abdul Jabbar, however, denied allegations of a fertiliser shortage or sales above the government-fixed price.
“There is no fertiliser shortage in the union where the incident occurred. We are trying to recover the fertiliser,” he said.
However, a mobile court led by Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) Amrit Deb Nath later found evidence supporting the farmers’ allegation that fertiliser was being sold to retail traders instead of farmers.
The mobile court fined a dealer Tk5,000 in Paglahat area of Shilkhuri Union over the allegation.
“We are conducting inspections at dealer points and retail markets, taking the farmers’ complaints seriously,” the UNO said.
Bhurungamari Police Station Officer-in-Charge Azim Uddin told the Dhaka Tribune that 197 sacks of fertiliser were taken away during the distribution.
“Fearing they would not get fertiliser, people who had come to collect it took away the sacks,” he said.
Police had recovered 58 sacks by the afternoon, he said, adding that legal action would be taken if the remaining fertiliser was not returned.

item.title: 136 unnatural deaths, 684 crime cases recorded in Satkhira
item.description:
A total of 136 unnatural deaths and 684 criminal cases were recorded in Satkhira between May and July, according to a quarterly report presented at a human rights advocacy meeting in the district on Saturday.
The report was prepared under the District Human Rights Defender Network (DHRNS) project of Uttaran with support from the Human Rights Culture Foundation (MSF). It also documented at least 33 incidents of human rights violations during the three-month period.
Advocate Muhammad Muniruddin, secretariat support staff of MSF, presented the report at a meeting held at Mangrove Conference Hall.
According to data from the Satkhira General Register Officer (GRO) office, the 684 cases included nine murders, 21 rape cases, 50 cases of violence against women, seven child abuse cases and six abductions. Other cases included robbery, dacoity, theft, housebreaking and vehicle theft.
A significant portion of the cases involved narcotics offences, with 251 filed under the Narcotics Control Act. There were also 12 cases under the Anti-Smuggling Act, five under the Cyber Security Act, three under the Arms Act, five under the Speedy Trial Act and four under the Pornography Control Act. The district recorded 632 criminal cases during the previous three-month period.
Of the 136 unnatural deaths, 49 occurred in May, 44 in June and 43 in July. The district also recorded 65 suicides during the period. A separate compilation based on local newspaper reports recorded 68 abnormal deaths, including 15 murders. The deaths included fatalities from road accidents, lightning, electrocution, drowning, storms and other incidents.
The report also raised concerns over security along the border and in the Sundarbans. Two Bangladeshis were reportedly injured in BSF firing along the border in June, while 32 fishermen were allegedly abducted for ransom while fishing in the Sundarbans.
Participants expressed concern over the prolonged absence of a judge at the Satkhira Women and Children Repression Prevention Tribunal, saying it had disrupted the filing and disposal of cases and delayed justice for women and children.
They decided to organize a human chain in front of the district court on August 30 and submit a memorandum to the senior district and sessions judge.
MSF Coordinator Sofia Hasin called for stronger monitoring, investigation, documentation and victim support to address human rights violations. She said every violation represents not merely a statistic but a person’s life, a family’s suffering and a failure of society and the state.
The meeting was chaired by Advocate Abul Kalam Azad, convener of the Satkhira District Human Rights Defender Network, and attended by human rights activists, lawyers, journalists and civil society representatives.

item.title: Land dispute stalls Pagla River bridge, 400,000 people suffer
item.description:
Construction of the 172.30-metre Bir Muktijoddha Dr Moin Uddin Ahmed Montu Bridge over the Pagla River in Shibganj upazila of Chapainawabganj has remained stalled for around five months due to land acquisition dispute, causing severe hardship to nearly 400,000 people in three unions.
The Tk29.99 crore bridge is being constructed by the Local Government Engineering Department (LGED) under the Important Bridges on Rural Roads (Second Phase) project. Work began on November 15, 2023, and the bridge was scheduled to be completed by November 14 this year. However, only about 60% of the construction has been completed so far.
The delay has forced residents of Monakasha, Binodpur and Durlabhpur unions to depend on an ageing Bailey bridge. The narrow, single-lane bridge frequently experiences traffic congestion, particularly during school hours and on market days. Heavy vehicles were banned from using it about three years ago because of safety concerns, with brick barriers installed at its entrance.
The situation has increased transportation costs for local traders. Traders from Durlabhpur and Monakasha now have to travel through Kansat, adding 20 to 30 kilometres to their journeys.
“Shibganj market is only three kilometres away, but we now have to travel around 30 kilometres by truck to bring goods,” said Shahin Ali, a grocery shopkeeper in Durlabhpur.
Students are also suffering because of the congestion. A ninth-grade student of Shibganj Government Model High School said traffic jams often caused students to arrive late, with the problem becoming particularly serious during examinations.
Harun-or-Rashid, a resident of Bakruli-Bishwanathpur village in Monakasha, recalled being stuck in traffic for around 30 minutes while travelling to the district town for urgent work. He eventually walked about two kilometres to Shibganj town, but the person he had gone to meet had already left.
The main obstacle to the new bridge is the acquisition of land needed for its approach road. According to local residents, 2.65 acres of land were acquired during construction of the Bailey bridge in 1991-92. Additional land is now required for the new bridge.
The eviction process involving at least 14 families has begun but remains incomplete. The Shibganj upazila administration issued eviction notices in November 2023 and March 2024. The affected residents subsequently appealed to the Deputy Commissioner, seeking suspension of the process.
Durlabhpur Union Parishad Chairman Mohammad Golam Azam said the dispute mainly concerned the validity of land documents. While the administration says compensation cannot be paid because some residents lack valid documents, the affected families claim they possess the necessary papers.
Abdul Haque, one of those served with an eviction notice, said his family had lived in the area for years. “Where will we go without compensation or rehabilitation?” he asked.
Other affected residents, including Bayezid and Tohurul Islam, said they were willing to leave if alternative accommodation was arranged. Sumaiya Khatun said the families had submitted their documents but the administration had yet to determine the value of their land.
Construction has reportedly been halted several times. Initially, residents obstructed the work over allegations of irregularities, but construction resumed after an investigation. Later, heavy rainfall and flooding disrupted the project. Work is now suspended because of the land dispute and the monsoon.
Mohammad Sahin Alam, manager of the construction company, denied rumours that the contractor had fled. Contractor Abdul Mannan also rejected allegations of negligence or irregularities, saying the bridge could be completed by December 2026 if the land complications were resolved.
Shibganj Upazila Engineer Mohammad Sahinul Islam said a key pier in the middle of the river could not be constructed during the monsoon. He added that the approach-road land had not yet been handed over to LGED.
LGED Executive Engineer Harun-or-Rashid said officials had conducted an on-site assessment and submitted a report to the Deputy Commissioner's office. He said work could resume quickly once the land acquisition and eviction processes were completed.
With the original completion deadline approaching, residents fear that further delays will prolong their dependence on the ageing Bailey bridge, increasing transport costs and worsening daily hardships across the three unions.

item.title: Gas flows again, crisis has years to run
item.description:
Gas supply has begun recovering with the arrival of fresh LNG cargoes, easing some of the severe shortages that disrupted power generation and industrial production across Bangladesh in recent weeks.
But the relief masks a much bigger problem: the country still faces a daily gas deficit of around 1.3 billion cubic feet, with no quick solution in sight.
Government projections suggest it could take at least two years before additional LNG infrastructure comes online, while declining domestic production and limited pipeline capacity mean even uninterrupted imports cannot fully bridge the gap.
The crisis, therefore, is shifting from an immediate question of when gas supply will improve to a more difficult one: when will Bangladesh actually have enough gas?
The country's gas demand currently stands at around 4 billion cubic feet per day (bcfd).
Even under normal conditions, however, supply can reach only around 2.6-2.7bcfd, roughly 1bcfd from imported LNG and another 1.6bcfd from domestic fields.
That leaves a structural shortfall of around 1.3bcfd even when the system is functioning normally.
The fragility of that system became evident after a fire at Excelerate Energy's LNG terminal in Moheshkhali on July 21.
The disruption reduced LNG supply, hitting power plants and industries and contributing to prolonged load-shedding and severe gas shortages.
Although the terminal was repaired, a subsequent shortage of LNG cargoes again constrained supply.
The situation has now improved.
LNG supply, which stood at around 580 million cubic feet on Saturday afternoon, rose to approximately 686 million cubic feet following the arrival of a new cargo.
Total gas supply has consequently climbed to around 2.3bcf per day.
But that still leaves the country about 1.7bcf short of estimated demand.
The government itself has warned consumers and industries not to expect a rapid end to the crisis.
Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury said on August 16 that the gas and electricity problems could not be permanently resolved within six months or a year.
“It will take at least two years,” he said, noting that constructing another floating LNG terminal could itself require around one and a half to two years.
The government is moving ahead with a third LNG terminal at Moheshkhali.
Chinese company CNEC has been selected for the project, but the contract has yet to be signed. The company has proposed completing construction within 22 months after signing.
Even more LNG terminals, however, would not automatically solve the problem.
Existing pipeline capacity from Moheshkhali towards Chittagong also constrains how much additional imported gas can be transported, meaning further terminals would require additional transmission infrastructure.
At the same time, domestic production continues to decline.
Bangladesh's gas fields have a stated daily production capacity of around 2.75bcf, but production on August 20-21 stood at only around 1.63bcf, about 59% of capacity.
Bibiyana, the country's largest producing gas field, alone is producing around 450 million cubic feet less per day than three years ago.
Power and Energy Minister Iqbal Hassan Mahmood Tuku has blamed years of inadequate exploration for increasing dependence on imports, saying the country would have been in a stronger position had exploration and LNG infrastructure been expanded earlier.
The government plans more FSRUs by 2029 alongside intensified domestic exploration.
Experts say Bangladesh cannot simply import its way out of the shortage.
Additional LNG terminals require not only infrastructure but also billions of dollars in recurring fuel imports.
Energy expert Professor M Shamsul Alam said major measures being undertaken now could take two to seven years to produce significant results.
He believes, however, that drilling five to six exploration wells annually and discovering commercially viable reserves could substantially reduce the shortage within five years.
Offshore exploration offers another possibility, but any major discovery there could take considerably longer to reach the national grid.
For now, therefore, fresh LNG cargoes can ease the immediate pain but cannot end the crisis.

item.title: Shamim: Freedom of expression for people of all faiths to be ensured
item.description:
Newly appointed State Minister for Religious Affairs Mohammad Shamim Kaiser on Sunday said utmost efforts will be made to ensure that people of all faiths and opinions can express their views freely from their respective positions.
He was exchanging views with journalists at the conference room of the Ministry of Religious Affairs at the Bangladesh Secretariat here on Sunday afternoon, said a press release.
The state minister said Bangladesh is unique because the overwhelming majority of its people are pious, describing the country as a land of communal harmony and religious people.
“If followers of every religion truly practice and uphold the teachings of their respective scriptures, communal harmony in the country will be strengthened further,” Shamim said.
Referring to the establishment of the Ministry of Religious Affairs, he said Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman had realized the need for a dedicated ministry for religious affairs in Bangladesh, while former prime minister Begum Khaleda Zia highly valued religious principles.
He said the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) has grown into a major political force because it placed importance on Bangladeshi nationalism and religious values, earning a place in the hearts of the country’s people.
Responding to a question regarding a statement issued by an organization over his appointment as state minister, Shamim said it was unrealistic to expect unanimous acceptance of any political decision or appointment by cent of the people.
“In any election, no political party receives the support of cent percent of the people. Likewise, no appointment will be liked by everyone. Sometimes, if an issue is not clearly explained or only partial information is circulated, misunderstandings may arise,” he added.
“Greater communication and discussions will help resolve any misunderstandings, InSha’Allah,” said the state minister. The state minister said he visited Jamia Madania Baridhara on Saturday and held discussions with several senior Islamic scholars associated with Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam and Hefazat-e-Islam Bangladesh.
“The Islamic scholars I sat with yesterday (Saturday) had some questions. I believe I was able to satisfy them. They welcomed me warmly,” he added.
Shamim said that the Ministry of Religious Affairs works with the coexistence and religious values of all prominent Islamic scholars of different views in Bangladesh.
“The ministry does not work only for Islam. I will reach out to leaders and spiritual guides of other religions as well. Any confusion that exists will be removed,” he added.
Religious Affairs Secretary Munshi Alauddin Al Azad, Islamic Foundation (IF) Director General Mohammad Mohibbullahil Baqee, and Additional Secretary (Hajj Wing) of the ministry Dr Md Ayatul Islam were present on the occasion, among others.
Earlier, the state minister exchanged views with officials of the ministry and organizations under it.

item.title: Can't provide electricity and gas overnight even if we want
item.description:
The government's six-month term has passed. During this time, the government has taken some steps and is preparing to take more. However, issues with gas and electricity have arisen anew. There is optimism about the revenue collection situation. There has been no visible progress in recovering embezzled money. At his residence in Gulshan last Friday, Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury talked about loans from the IMF, the investment situation, the stock market, a new pay structure for government employees, etc. The interview was conducted by Special Correspondent Fakhrul Islam.

Prothom Alo: Why did you change the fiscal year? What will be the benefit?

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: The fiscal year had been July-June all along. Now it will be April-March. When the fiscal year starts in July, it's the monsoon season. We noticed that preparation is done during the dry season, but work starts in the monsoon, delaying budget implementation. Most work is done towards the end, meaning a significant amount of time is lost in preparation. Now, work can be done in full swing during the dry season, making project implementation much easier. Previously, work had to start in water, leading to wastage and corruption. We used to say that money went in the water, and this is similar. Many times, money released at the last moment would literally end up in water. We decided on a new fiscal year to avoid this.

Prothom Alo: Was any study or analysis conducted before this decision was taken?

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: Why is that necessary? Everything is already in our hands. We can see everything. With this new decision, we expect project implementation to be much faster, reducing waste and corruption.

Prothom Alo: When you took charge six months ago, what was the state of the economy, and in which indicators are we better off now? We want to know about both successes and failures. What challenges are you facing, and where are the obstacles?

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: Let's talk about the successes first. Firstly, the foreign currency reserve was 34. 02 billion dollars on 15 February. By 13 August, it increased to 37.11 billion. The balance of payments was 2.28 billion dollars surplus on 26 January, and it rose to 6.61 billion dollars by 26 July. As we all know, remittance growth continues. The policy interest rate has been reduced from 10 per cent to 9.5 per cent. Interbank transaction rates and other interest rates are also decreasing. Public confidence is returning to the banking system. There has been significant growth in bank deposits. We have somewhat been able to prevent capital flight. Necessary measures have been taken to discourage the culture of loan defaults. A strict stance has been taken towards establishing accountability in the banking sector. The government's and Bangladesh Bank's measures to prevent bad loans from increasing further are starting to work. I believe there has been good progress in the financial sector over these six months.

Prothom Alo: What are the failures then?

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: The first thing I would mention is inflation. We have reduced it a bit in July, but we still don't think it's under control. It needs to be reduced further. Secondly, private sector investment and loan growth have not increased as expected. Thirdly, the problems with gas and electricity persist. We haven't reached the desired level of industrial production. These issues are interconnected; we can't just increase electricity production or gas supply overnight. It will take time. But external pressures have caused us significant harm. Unfortunately, the war in the Middle East started within a week of us taking office, leading to increased prices for all goods. The impact of rising oil and gas prices on productivity is inevitable.

Prothom Alo: You did not mention what you are unable to do due to obstacles?

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: No, there is no opportunity to face any obstruction. We are an elected government. We have a manifesto and promises to the people. Our first task is to fully deliver on these promises, which we are implementing one by one. There will always be both positive and negative aspects to the economy. But we will continue to fulfill our fundamental responsibilities to the citizens.

Prothom Alo: The interim government had undertaken several initiatives, such as making the exchange rate more market-based, merging five banks, dividing the NBR into two parts, listing business groups for recovering embezzled funds internationally, and enacting a Bank Resolution Act. Which of these initiatives do you not support, meaning which, if absent, could have been better and are now your responsibility to carry?

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: We are implementing these fully. However, they did some things halfway, making it cumbersome for us and giving us a hard time. They couldn't manage these matters well. For instance, NBR was divided into two halves incompletely, creating some problems, and now we're fixing them. For this reason, we haven't passed the related bill yet. If tax policy isn't determined accurately and by the right person, it impacts the overall tax system. We are aware of this. Therefore, we decided the creators of tax policy won't exclusively be bureaucratic; there will be a team of experts. Discussions will happen not just internally but also with stakeholders. There will be evaluations of how tax policy impacts inflation, living standards, and the environment. But the interim government left it in a way where many complications have arisen. I'm hesitant to articulate these issues. The work is progressing - the NBR will be divided into two.

Prothom Alo: And the merger of five banks and other issues?

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: That was also half-done. I can't discuss whether it's for good or bad now. The Bank Resolution issue is very tough. There's nearly Tk 2 trillion deficit. It's tough for the government alone to cover that. Significant embezzlement happened abroad too. Perhaps this could have been handled better. Since it has happened, our duty now is to see how we can implement it properly. We're working on it, Insha'Allah. We'll manage, but it'll take time. There's no need to debate whether it could have been done differently now. Our priority is to ensure depositors' funds remain protected. A clause in the Bank Resolution was included, that has been cancelled, but all else remains intact. The exchange rate is almost market-based.

Prothom Alo: Will depositors in the five banks, those who had deposited 10 one crore, two crores, or five crores, get their money back?

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: We are working on ensuring that with full vigour. If we can't provide security to the depositors, and they lose faith in the banking sector, then the economy won’t operate. We will implement this, even if it takes some time.

Prothom Alo: Which type of depositors are you referring to? Small or large?

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: Depositors mean depositors. There's no issue of big or small here. Again, stating that whoever has deposited in the bank, if their funds aren't protected within this banking system, the public will lose faith. So our initiatives are for everyone, not just the small or large ones. Many people have deposited their lifetime earnings with great difficulty in the bank; I hope we will succeed in returning it.

Prothom Alo: You have often discussed economic reforms and deregulation after assuming office as Finance Minister. How much have you managed to achieve?

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: This too is a challenging task. The problem is so ingrained in the culture of Bangladesh that removing it by its roots will take time, as it's entangled with corrupt businessmen and government officials. But we are committed to doing it. Without this, we won't be able to transform the economy in the direction we envision. We can't achieve economic democratisation which we're advocating without deregulation. Investment won't come without deregulation, which in turn won't generate employment, or fuel economic growth. For years, the country became overly regulated due to the favour-based economy.

Prothom Alo: Ordinary people assess government success by market prices, income, and employment. In these six months, have people seen any real changes in any of these three?

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: The employment package announced for Tk 650 billion aims to enhance employment. Small and medium industries produce more employment. The policy rate has been reduced. Inflation has slightly decreased. A quasi-market-based exchange rate is functioning. Nearly 12-13 thousand jobs have been added within the banking sector itself. We've deregulated and relaxed tariff rates to attract investment. The initiatives we've taken according to our manifesto, and those to be taken, if implemented fully, will foster employment, growth, and reduced inflation.

Prothom Alo: Between boosting growth and reducing inflation, which would you prioritise?

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: We need to achieve both - growth and controlled inflation. International factors affect inflation, which we can't control. Inside the country, if we can cut business costs and create a business-friendly environment, we'll undoubtedly see positive results. Previously, due to corruption and the tax system, people faced hardships.

Prothom Alo: Why should someone invest in Bangladesh?

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: Investment has occurred in Bangladesh. Both local and foreign investors have stepped in. But without moving away from patronage politics, genuine investors might hesitate. We have managed to cultivate that environment. Our message is clear—there's no room for patronage anymore. We've created and will continue to create an environment where everyone can participate and benefit from the economy.

Even the stock market, which faced major issues, corruption, and embezzlement, won't face the same troubles again. It had turned into something akin to a casino. No reputable company will enter a casino-like market. With the environment we're crafting, a new commission formed, and restored public trust in this commission, we see the stock market is gaining traction. Companies are motivated to enlist.

There's another matter too—there's a connection between the banking sector and the stock market. The stock market had collapsed in the past. Everyone was forced to take loans from banks. This shouldn’t be. Massive loans at high interests—how feasible is that? Banks took short-term deposits to offer long-term loans. This scenario shouldn't occur. The arena for large financing is the stock market. Banks should furnish working capital.

Prothom Alo: When can we see this scenario where the stock market handles large financing and banks manage working capital?

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: One can't set a date for the economy. For creating momentum in the economy, we have taken many steps, laws have changed and will change further. Restored trust in the stock market is important. Since changing the commission, trust has returned.

Prothom Alo: Why didn't you change it sooner? Trust would have returned earlier.

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: Appointments take time. Rushed appointments can't be granted. We worked for three months to ensure appointments. We've decided not to appoint anyone political to the financial sector. Expertise, integrity were checked before appointments, and once made, people saw they were justly appointed.

Prothom Alo: Recently, former leaders from Chhatra Dal and Juba Dal have been appointed as chairmen of various corporations or entities.

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: Those are fine. I referred to the financial sector. However, proper audits will now proceed in these organisations too. Previously, audits weren't conducted properly.

Prothom Alo: You were discussing investment and employment. You're aware of the low loan growth in the private sector. Rather than offer to entrepreneurs, some state-owned banks like Sonali are investing heavily in treasury bonds. Is this their responsibility?

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: You've pointed at the right spot. I am aware and am stopping it. We'll set a liments in treasury bonds, in reality, it's weak performance.

Prothom Alo: Despite relief in dollar markets and reserves, imports of capital machinery and raw materials are declining. Private sector loan growth is at its lowest, and businessmen are waiting for new investment decisions even after six months. How long will this wait last?

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: From both the Awami League and the interim government, we inherited a colossal problem. This isn't something that can be corrected overnight. We're trying to exit this problem promptly, but it will take time. We are in a transition from a patronage-based model to democratisation. We've gained some results from the initiatives taken. The private sector is highly encouraged by our policy measures. We have received full support for the budget from the private sector. They have warmly received this budget. You've seen that after the budget, commodity prices haven't spiked.

Prothom Alo: You mention reducing the interest rate for policy loans. Is this enough for investment amidst crises in gas and electricity, extortion, weak law enforcement, and bureaucratic complexities? Will lower policy rates alone attract investments?

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: You're correct, I agree with you. However, my argument is to follow the trajectory of the economy. Is it heading downward? It's not. We are encouraging entrepreneurs to touch the stock market. Taking loans from the stock market incurs no huge interests. If profits occur, they will pay dividends. We've simplified direct listing - applications previously lying for years will now be processed within three months. Roughly 20 companies lean toward listing. The remaining challenges will take some time.

Prothom Alo: You mentioned a two-year timeline to overcome the gas and electricity crisis and a two-year timeline to tackle economic stagnation to establish complete recovery within four years. What are the interim plans to increase production, restart closed factories, boost investments, increase employment, and control inflation during this period?

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: I referred to transitions from fragile to stable and finally to prosperity in two years and four years. This will proceed sequentially. Unfortunately, the 18-month tenure of the interim government wasted much of our time. During that period, they barely focused on gas sectors. The time went to waste, causing substantial harm. They dragged the country further down during that long pause. Now we have to do everything all at once.

Prothom Alo: Did you equate the interim government's tenure with that of the Awami League?

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: Yes. Add the interim period of a year and a half with the Awami League’s 15 and a half years, making 17 years of clutter to clean up and advance the economy. We need to pull it out of the pit first, then stabilise it before the economy gains true momentum. You will see that the economy will take off by the fourth or fifth year. We are doing all the policy work, reformations, and receiving positive feedback. Foreign fund managers are coming. We expect to bring in 2 billion US dollars from Hong Kong. Confidence in the economy is growing.

Prothom Alo: In the recovery of bad loans and embezzled funds over the last six months, how visible is the progress?

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: We've identified about 70 to 80 thousand crore takas (Tk 700 billion to 800 billion) of embezzled funds. We are still trying to identify more. Work is ongoing. If I say money will be returned shortly, it will be misinformation. Extracting those funds from embezzled host countries is challenging. The governments of those countries may not cooperate, nor do those who have the money. However, recovery efforts continue. Those who think they can embezzle and enjoy abroad will be disappointed. Recovery attempts will persist till the last day. Some results will be noticed.

Prothom Alo: The electoral manifesto includes promises of forming a commission for financial sector reform and abolishing the Financial Institutions Division under the Ministry of Finance. Do you still hold that position?

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: Certainly. We're progressing with our reforms. In the budget, most of our reform steps have been introduced. The commission's task was deregulation, which we fulfilled largely now. For the rest, if feedback indicates issues, they can be addressed too. The matter of the Financial Institutions Division is still a part of our thinking. The economy is so delicate that closing it will not result in a stronger economy tomorrow morning. I need a good position before heading that way. Still, what we said is on our mind. Once the economy stabilises, we'll tackle that.

Prothom Alo: The government backed away from the earlier IMF programme because it didn't align with national interests. Which conditions were objected to? In the new IMF programme, what reforms are required? Should conditions arise to cut subsidies, raise taxes, or increase power and energy prices, what will be the government's position?

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: Our primary responsibility remains towards the people. Globally except for us, almost all countries have raised electricity prices. Due to the energy crisis, they have raised oil prices; the US prices doubled, Sri Lanka's by 25 per cent. People's purchasing power has dwindled. Initially, we were reluctant to raise prices until the very end. After that, there remains the subsidy. Removing the oil subsidy would increase electricity prices four to five times—is that acceptable to Bangladeshi citizens? Could they afford it? They’re providing their statements, and so are we, stating that we'll execute everything but with sequencing. In today's economic backdrop, making such moves is tough. Eventually, we'll head in that direction, but our economy must first reach a certain point.

Prothom Alo: What's the status of the IMF's new loan programme?

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: We exited the previous IMF programme. There's no benefit in accepting IMF loans contrary to our national and public interest. The past fascist Sheikh Hasina government accepted everything. They had no responsibility toward the public. But we do, as an elected government. We've told them to drop the previous one and develop a new programme. The updates on the new programme are being done; discussions will begin. We've stated that everything will be done, but the sequence must be different. Discussions on the new programme will commence anew.

Prothom Alo: Can it be a situation where, if the IMF conditions aren’t met, then the loan won't be available?

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: Let's see. The loan isn't too significant. We've provided an electoral manifesto. The public believed in us, which is most important for me.

Prothom Alo: On one side, you're indicating a shortfall in the government treasury, while on the other, you plan for a new pay structure and a large development budget. Where will the funding come from? Many think this will increase debt or inflationary pressure. What's your opinion?

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: Look, our tax to GDP ratio is one of the lowest globally. With the initiatives taken, we hope tax collection will increase. Previously, inefficiency, lack of governance, and corruption plagued tax collection, which we're rectifying. You've seen good collection in the fourth quarter of the last fiscal year. We're striving for transparency in this regard, and the message has spread. We expect to meet our target. We're noticing signs. Management is strengthening. NBR will become two parts. Collectively, I can say we won't need excessive borrowing. We'll explore alternative financing modes, as the government always borrows from the banking sector, often depriving the private sector.

Prothom Alo: Where will funding come from for the new pay structure?

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: We can't provide it all at once.

Prothom Alo: Even in two installments, it's a hefty sum.

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: Not even in two. We're working on this. Calculations are ongoing. Due to massive imports, revenue space has significantly shrunk. Even with intent, we can't release everything at once.

Prothom Alo: Will the announcement to give from July this year be upheld?

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: As I mentioned, we're working on this.

Prothom Alo: You're elected for five years; six months have passed. What is the plan for the remaining four and a half years? What's the message?

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury: The message is we're navigating carefully and accurately. We ask for cooperation to successfully democratise the economy, as intended. We're transitioning from a challenging state, and government alone can't achieve this. A collective effort is needed.

item.title: Low pressure forms over sea, caution signal at 4 ports
item.description:
A low-pressure system has formed over the Bay of Bengal, prompting the Bangladesh Meteorological Department to ask four seaports to hoist Local Cautionary Signal no. 3. The warning was issued late on Sunday night.

However, meteorologists said the likelihood of the system developing into a depression remains low. It is also unlikely to bring heavy rainfall.

Rainfall may increase today, Monday, particularly in coastal areas, while parts of the capital may receive some rain between the afternoon and evening.

Two low-pressure systems have already formed this month, although neither brought significant rainfall. Meteorologist Md Omar Faruk of the Bangladesh Meteorological Department said the latest system is also unlikely to intensify into a depression.

Low-pressure over Bay: Maritime ports asked to hoist cautionary signal No. 3

Speaking to Prothom Alo this morning, he said, “A low-pressure system is currently situated over the north-western Bay of Bengal and adjoining areas. Under its influence, coastal areas may experience intermittent rainfall. Rainfall may increase somewhat, which could bring temporary relief.”

The weather bulletin advised fishing boats and trawlers operating in the North Bay to remain close to the coast and navigate cautiously until further notice.

According to a warning issued by the Storm Warning Centre yesterday, Sunday, strong winds may sweep across the seaports, the North Bay and Bangladesh’s coastal areas under the influence of the low-pressure system.

Consequently, Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Mongla and Payra seaports have been asked to hoist Local Cautionary Signal no. 3.

Meteorologist Omar Faruk said, “This low-pressure system is unlikely to have any significant impact on Bangladesh. Although scattered rainfall may occur this week, prolonged rainfall is unlikely. However, rainfall may increase next Sunday. Another low-pressure system may also form two days later.”

He added, “The capital may receive rain in the afternoon or evening today. However, the rainfall is unlikely to be heavy.”

The weather bulletin also said that temperatures may fall slightly today, Monday compared with yesterday, Sunday.

item.title: Brazil want to play Bangladesh in October
item.description:
The arrival of a five-member Brazilian delegation directly from the airport at the National Stadium yesterday, Sunday, followed by an inspection of everything from the pitch and dressing rooms to the stands and media box, has fuelled hopes of a major possibility.

Now, that possibility appears to be gaining momentum. Brazil’s national football team wants to come to Dhaka and play against Bangladesh after the FIFA ASEAN Cup.

Brazil to play in Kolkata on 3 October

The September FIFA international window will end on 6 October. Within that period, the Brazilian Football Confederation (CBF) has proposed playing a friendly against Bangladesh at the National Stadium in Dhaka. A responsible source from Bangladesh Football Federation (BFF) said this to Prothom Alo.

Brazil have proposed holding the match on either 5 or 6 October. The five-time world champions want to travel to Dhaka with a delegation of around 90 people to play the match against Bangladesh.

The ASEAN Cup final will be held in Indonesia on 3 October. The tournament begins on 24 September, and Bangladesh are scheduled to play three group-stage matches. Taking the national team’s busy schedule into consideration, the BFF has not yet given Brazil a final response.

A five-member Brazilian delegation arrived in Dhaka yesterday as part of preparations for their tour of India. They travelled directly from the airport to the National Stadium. After inspecting almost the entire stadium, they also visited Bashundhara Kings Arena. Later that evening, they met BFF president Tabith Awal.

Brazil could play friendly in Kolkata, Bangladesh also in discussion

Brazil will play a friendly against India’s national team in Kolkata on 3 October. The Indian Football Federation had originally withdrawn from the FIFA ASEAN Cup mainly to accommodate this match. FIFA subsequently invited Bangladesh to take India’s place.

Brazil’s national football team have never visited Bangladesh. On 6 September 2011, Lionel Messi’s Argentina came to Dhaka to play a friendly against Nigeria at the National Stadium.

item.title: Pakistan’s army chief to visit Iran with war mediation stalled
item.description:
PAKISTAN-SYRIA-DIPLOMACY

Pakistan’s powerful army chief Asim Munir will travel to Tehran on Monday, Iran’s foreign ministry said, as Islamabad tries to mediate a resolution to the Middle East war.

Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said in a statement Sunday that Munir would lead a delegation to the Iranian capital “as part of efforts to strengthen Iran-Pakistan bilateral cooperation”.

The visit was also part of “Pakistan’s ongoing efforts to help consolidate peace and security in the region”, the statement said.

Pakistan has played a key role in efforts to halt war between Iran and the United States, brokering a memorandum of understanding in June, but peace negotiations currently appear stalled.

Earlier this month Pakistan signed a joint defence agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkey, a move some analysts said was aimed at countering Iranian influence.

item.title: Oil falls as Trump pledges economic war on Iran
item.description:
Oil prices fell on Monday as investors braced for details of a US plan to isolate the Iranian economy that President Donald Trump billed as the "most crushing" financial operation ever against Tehran.
Asian stocks were mostly down in early trading, with South Korea's tech-rich Kospi falling 1.4% after Samsung Electronics said it spent a massive $80 billion to buy back its own shares following weeks of turbulent trading.
The chip giant's shares, along with those of rival SK hynix, peaked in June on optimism for the artificial intelligence boom, but have since fallen amid investor jitters and a broader tech rout.
In an important week for artificial intelligence, investors are also looking towards an earnings report from Nvidia, the world's most valuable company and a bellwether for the sector.
The recurring question for the US chip maker is whether the AI boom will continue to accelerate as the technology takes over more corners of the broader economy.
"The spending machine is still running, but the bill is getting heavier," said Stephen Innes of SPI Asset Management.
"Nvidia must now show that the most expensive investment boom in modern market history can still pay its bills."
Chinese tech giant Alibaba is also keeping focus on the sector this week after announcing on Sunday that it plans to issue $10.2 billion in new shares in Hong Kong to fund its global AI ambitions.
The firm, known for its open-source "Qwen" AI models, has been ploughing tens of billions of dollars into artificial intelligence, with its shareholders eager to see how it will monetise the huge investments.
Tokyo, Shanghai, Taipei and Wellington were down on Monday. Sydney, Jakarta and Bangkok posted gains, while Manila and Kuala Lumpur were flat.
Eyes are also on US Treasury boss Scott Bessent, who he would give more details in a news conference on Monday on a fresh push to pile economic pressure on Iran.
The United States warned allies and China on Thursday to join Trump's new campaign, which comes as the unpopular war in the Middle East drags toward the six-month mark.
Vice President JD Vance admitted the plan was a "delicate dance" because Iran will "try to apply economic pressure to us".
Asked whether the United States would pressure China, Bessent told CNBC that "many conversations are best to have in private", but called on Beijing "to get with the program".
Both main crude contracts were down 2.3%, with the Brent benchmark sitting at $92 a barrel.
Traders will also be watching this week's annual gathering of central bankers, economists and finance chiefs in Jackson Hole in the United States, hoping for some clarification on US monetary policy.
The meeting comes after the Treasury bought its own bonds last week in an effort to push down borrowing costs after the 30-year yield surged to levels last seen in 2007, just before the global financial crisis.
Yields have risen on inflation fears and as the United States reported that its federal debt had topped $40 trillion.

item.title: Dhaka ranks 18th in global air quality ranking
item.description:
Dhaka ranked 18th among the world’s most polluted cities on Monday morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 87.
The city’s air quality was classified as ‘moderate’, according to the AQI scale.
Malaysia’s Kuching topped the list with an AQI of 194, followed by Pakistan's Lahore with 170, and Indonesia'a Jakarta with 167.
Kampala, capital of Uganda, was also among the cities with the highest pollution levels.
An AQI between 50 and 100 is considered "moderate" with an acceptable air quality while AQI between 101 and 150 is considered ‘unhealthy for sensitive groups’, while a score between 151 and 200 is classified as ‘unhealthy’. AQI readings between 201 and 300 are termed ‘very unhealthy’, and anything above 301 is considered ‘hazardous’, posing serious health risks.
The AQI is a daily indicator of air quality, showing how clean or polluted the air is and the possible health effects people may experience.
In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five major pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide and ozone.
Dhaka has long struggled with severe air pollution. Air quality usually worsens during winter and improves in the monsoon season.
According to the World Health Organization, air pollution causes around seven million deaths globally each year, mainly from stroke, heart disease, chronic respiratory diseases, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

item.title: Shoriful joins Ambrose in rare feat on Australian soil
item.description:
Bangladesh left-arm pacer Shoriful Islam produced a remarkable performance in the second Test against Australia amid his side’s innings and 51-run defeat as he became the first bowler in 33 years after West Indies legend Curtly Ambrose to take seven wickets in a Test innings on Australian soil.
Shoriful's figures marked his maiden five-wicket haul in Test cricket and the best bowling performance by a Bangladeshi bowler outside the country. His 7-48 is also the best figures by a Bangladesh bowler against Australia and by a Bangladeshi fast bowler in Test cricket.
In doing so, he became the first visiting bowler since Ambrose in 1993 to claim seven wickets in a Test innings on Australian soil.
Ambrose took seven for 25 against Australia at the WACA Ground in Perth in 1993. At one stage of that spell, the West Indies great had taken seven wickets while conceding only one run.
The left-arm seamer troubled Australia's batters with sharp bouncers and late in swing.
Before this Test, Shoriful hadn’t even a five-wicket haul but his excellent bowling earned him a place in the history.
However, despite his record bowling, Australia managed to put up 210 and took a 146-run. Bangladesh were bowled out for 64 in the first innings, before being all out for 95 in the second innings to taste an innings and 51-run defeat inside two days.

More than 15,000 suicides reported each year
item.description:
Suicide has emerged as a major public health problem in Bangladesh. According to police records, 76,361 people died by suicide between 2020 and 2024—an average of more than 15,000 a year. That is more than three times the World Health Organization (WHO)’s estimated figure for Bangladesh in 2021.

Young people are at relatively higher risk of suicide. Family and relationship conflicts, psychological distress, depression, unemployment, academic pressure and examinations, among other social, economic and mental health factors, can increase the risk. Experts say reliable data collection, accessible mental health services and restrictions on access to lethal means such as pesticides are essential for suicide prevention.

These issues were discussed at a suicide prevention meeting held at the International Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research, Bangladesh (icddr,b) in Dhaka on Sunday.

The meeting was organised jointly by the National Institute of Mental Health and Hospital, the World Health Organization and icddr,b under the WHO’s suicide prevention project, “Live Life: Suicide Prevention in Bangladesh.” Mental health and psychiatric specialists, researchers, police officials and representatives of various ministries attended the event.

Participants also recommended repealing or reforming the law that criminalises attempted suicide. Several speakers said people who attempt suicide are usually in deep distress and need treatment, support and compassion rather than punishment.

A deeply rooted problem

In the first presentation, Mohammad Sohel Shamik, deputy project coordinator of icddr,b’s Maternal and Child Health Division, highlighted the scale of the problem. He said the number of suicides recorded by Bangladesh Police was much higher than the WHO’s estimated figure. According to the WHO’s latest estimate, for 2021, around 4,714 people die by suicide in Bangladesh each year. Police records, however, indicate 14,000 to 15,000 suicides annually.

Participants were given a draft of the National Suicide Prevention Strategy 2026–2030. It contains suicide statistics for 2020–2024 and January–October 2025. The number of suicides was lowest in 2024, at 13,975, and highest in 2022, at 16,886. In 2021, there were 15,774 suicides—more than three times the WHO estimate. These deaths are generally recorded by police stations as unnatural deaths, with cases filed accordingly.

According to police data, the highest number of suicides occurred in Jashore. Between 2022 and 2025, 1,454 cases involving suicide were filed there. The other nine districts with relatively high numbers were Dhaka, Cumilla, Dinajpur, Bogura, Mymensingh, Kushtia, Pabna, Jhenaidah and Naogaon.

Mohammad Sohel Shomik and several other participants said not all suicides or suicide attempts are reported or recorded. There are also instances in which killings are reported as suicides.

Under Section 309 of the Penal Code, attempting suicide is a punishable offence, carrying a maximum sentence of one year’s simple imprisonment, a fine, or both. In cases of suicide resulting in death, police conduct an unnatural-death inquiry under Section 174 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. If someone is found to have abetted or assisted a suicide, Section 306 of the Penal Code provides for up to 10 years’ imprisonment and a fine.

In the second presentation, Anika Tasnim Hossain, an associate scientist at icddr,b’s Maternal and Child Health Division, said fear and stigma were among the reasons suicide and suicide attempts were underreported.

She said data on suicides and suicide attempts could be collected from three sources: hospitals and clinics, police stations and communities. Community members often have the best knowledge of such incidents, she said. Teachers, imams, village police officers, medicine-shop owners and agricultural extension officers could be important sources of information.

Combining information from these three sources would provide a more accurate picture, she said.

Anika Tasnim Hossain said a pilot project on the issue was being implemented in four upazilas under the WHO project: Shibganj in Chapainawabganj, Gowainghat in Sylhet, Abhaynagar in Jashore and Shailkupa in Jhenaidah.

Compassion instead of punishment

Professor Fowara Tasnim, additional director general (development and research) of the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) and chief guest at the event, said there needed to be serious consideration of whether attempted suicide could be removed from the list of criminal offences. If that was not possible, she said, the law should be reformed.

There is no provision for legal action against a person who dies by suicide. However, participants said the law provides for punishment of people who survive a suicide attempt. The provision was introduced during British rule. Although Britain has since repealed the law, it remains in Bangladesh and most countries around the world no longer criminalise attempted suicide.

Several psychiatrists and mental health specialists at the event said mental health problems increase the risk of suicide and suicide attempts. Mental health problems should not be treated as criminal behaviour, they said. People who survive suicide attempts should receive medical care and compassion rather than punishment.

Two physicians from the National Institute of Mental Health and Hospital argued for retaining some form of punishment, saying authorities should also consider cases in which threats of suicide are used to blackmail or pressure others.

Additional Deputy Inspector General of Police (Crime Metro) Md Ashraful Islam said the existence of the law deterred some people from attempting suicide. He claimed that one reason suicide rates were lower among government employees was that they knew an attempt could lead to a year in prison and seriously damage their careers.

Participants cited a study conducted across 171 countries which found that criminalising suicide attempts was associated with higher suicide rates. They also said suicide rates had fallen in Sri Lanka and Singapore after attempts were decriminalised.

Restricting access to pesticides

Pesticides, insecticides and herbicides are among the major means of suicide in Bangladesh. Most are used in agriculture, but there is little regulation or monitoring of their use.

They are readily available, and people often leave them unsecured after using them in fields, creating a risk for those experiencing psychological distress.

Participants said suicide rates had been reduced in Sri Lanka and South Korea after certain pesticides and herbicides were banned. Mohammad Sohel Shomik of icddr,b said that in some parts of India, farmers did not have direct access to pesticides.

Instead, pesticides were obtained and used collectively through cooperatives, with village councils overseeing and monitoring their use. This had helped reduce suicides among farmers, he said.

The event opened with remarks by Md Anisur Rahman, senior director of icddr,b’s Maternal and Child Health Division. WHO National Professional Officer Hasina Momtaz then said young people appeared to face a higher risk of suicide and that their vulnerabilities needed to be better understood. She also stressed the importance of responsible reporting by the media.

In her closing remarks, Professor Safiun Nahar, director of the National Institute of Mental Health and chair of the event, said policy reform was necessary and difficult, but pesticide regulation was achievable. Authorities needed to ensure that pesticides did not become easily accessible to everyone, she said.

item.title: IUB Beatrice Tinsley research scholarship for Women Researchers, information needed to know
item.description:
To increase women’s participation in science and research and facilitate access to higher education, the Centre for Astronomy, Space Science and Astrophysics (CASSA) at Independent University, Bangladesh (IUB) has launched the “Beatrice Tinsley Postbac Research Assistantship”.

It offers a unique opportunity for emerging women researchers with an interest in science.

Under an IUB-funded sponsored research grant, the fellowship will appoint two full-time research assistants.

The one-year paid fellowship programme is primarily designed for women who have already completed their bachelor’s degree and intend to pursue a higher graduate degree, such as a master’s or PhD, in the future.

Jannatul’s higher education dream comes true, receives Tk 7.4m scholarship

Selected researchers will have the opportunity to work full-time under the one-year fellowship during 2026–27. During this period, each Tinsley Research Associate will receive a monthly stipend of Tk 30,000.

Throughout the year-long programme, fellows will take part in original research, with the principal objective of publishing a full research paper as the first author based on their own research.

From Haor to Sheffield, story of Shamsul Alam of receiving 3 scholarships

The assistantship will also directly support fellows in developing strong application profiles to pursue higher education at internationally recognised graduate schools.

Candidates with strong academic merit and a keen interest in research can apply online. Full details of the application process and the official form are available at cassa.bd/tra.

For queries regarding the application process or the fellowship, applicants are advised to contact the programme directly by email at kasad@iub.edu.bd.

The fellowship programme is expected to serve as a milestone in the future careers of young women aspiring to pursue higher education and build careers in science and research.

item.title: Verdict on death references, appeals in Nusrat murder case today
item.description:
The High Court will deliver its verdict today, Monday, on the death references and appeals filed by the convicts in the Nusrat Jahan murder case. A High Court bench comprising Justice Bhishmadev Chakraborty and Justice KM Rasheduzzaman Raja will pronounce the verdict.

Police have tightened security at Nusrat Jahan’s family home in Sonagazi, Feni, ahead of the verdict.

Sonagazi Model Police Station officer-in-charge Abul Hasim said security was increased following a request from Nusrat’s brother and case complainant, Mahmudul Hasan. Two police officers had been deployed at the house since the murder.

Seven more officers were deployed there from Sunday, he said. Surveillance has also been increased in the area to maintain law and order.

The High Court concluded hearings on the death references, appeals and jail appeals in the case on 20 August and set Monday for the verdict.

Nusrat’s elder brother Mahmudul Hasan said, “My parents and the rest of my family want justice. We hope the lower court’s verdict will be upheld by the High Court as well.” He said the family was satisfied with the additional security but was “not completely free of concern” because family members have to leave the house for various reasons.

Nusrat murder: Charges against ex-Sonagazi OC found true

The Chief Justice formed the special bench on 10 June to hear death references, appeals and other matters under laws relating to violence against women and children on a priority basis.

The bench began proceedings on 14 June. Hearings in the Nusrat murder case began on 28 July and continued for 17 working days.

The case

According to court records, on 27 March 2019, Siraj Ud Daula, then principal of Sonagazi Islamia Fazil (Degree) Madrasah, summoned Nusrat to his office and sexually harassed her. He was arrested after a case was filed.

On 6 April, after Nusrat refused to withdraw the case, she was taken to the madrasah rooftop, where her hands and feet were tied, kerosene was poured over her and she was set on fire. She died on 10 April while undergoing treatment at the burn unit of Dhaka Medical College Hospital.

Her elder brother Mahmudul Hasan filed a case over the arson at Sonagazi police station. It was later converted into a murder case.

In its verdict on 24 October 2019, the Feni Women and Children Repression Prevention Tribunal sentenced all 16 accused to death, including the suspended madrasah principal Siraj Ud Daula.

Sonagazi AL chief arrested over Nusrat murder

The other death-row convicts are Ruhul Amin, then president of Sonagazi upazila Awami League; Sonagazi municipality councillor Maksudul Alam; madrasah teacher Hafez Abdul Kader; lecturer Afsar Uddin; madrasah students Nur Uddin, Shahadat Hossain Shamim, Saifur Rahman Mohammad Zubayer, Javed Hossain alias Sakhawat Hossain Javed, Kamrun Nahar Moni, Umme Sultana Popy alias Tuhin, Abdur Rahim Sharif, Iftekhar Uddin Rana, Imran Hossain Mamun, Mohammad Shamim and Mahi Uddin Shakil.

After the trial court verdict, the case records were sent to the relevant High Court section on 29 October 2019 for a death reference and registered as Death Reference No. 140/2019.

A paper book was prepared on a priority basis because the case was considered sensational. The convicts also filed separate appeals and jail appeals.
